reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Presents as a groin lump located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, in contrast to an inguinal hernia which lies above and medial to it
More common in women than men, particularly in older and multiparous women, though inguinal hernia remains the commonest groin hernia overall in both sexes
The femoral canal has a narrow, rigid neck bounded by the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, and femoral vein, which makes strangulation far more likely than with inguinal hernias
A high proportion of femoral hernias present as an emergency with incarceration or strangulation rather than as an elective referral
A Richter's hernia, where only part of the bowel wall is trapped, can strangulate while the lumen stays patent, so bowel obstruction may be absent despite ischaemia
Because of the high strangulation risk, femoral hernias should generally be repaired promptly rather than managed conservatively
Repair may be performed by low (crural), high (McEvedy), or laparoscopic approaches, closing the femoral canal
A small, deep femoral hernia can be easily missed on examination, especially in obese patients
reference.pathophysiology: A femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, the medial-most compartment of the femoral sheath, below the inguinal ligament. The canal normally contains fat and a lymph node (node of Cloquet) and has an unyielding boundary. Raised intra-abdominal pressure forces peritoneum and abdominal contents through the femoral ring into this confined space. The rigidity and narrowness of the neck predispose trapped contents to incarceration and rapid compromise of blood supply, causing strangulation and bowel ischaemia. The sac may turn upward over the inguinal ligament, mimicking an inguinal hernia.
additionalDifferentials: Enlarged inguinal or femoral lymph node
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical localisation relative to the pubic tubercle
Ultrasound of the groin to confirm the diagnosis and characterise contents
CT abdomen and pelvis in obstruction or when the diagnosis is unclear
Bloods including lactate if strangulation is suspected
redFlags: Irreducible tender groin lump below the inguinal ligament indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency)
Signs of small bowel obstruction with a femoral lump
Localised ischaemia despite absent obstruction in a Richter's-type hernia
Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting perforation of strangulated bowel
reference.prognosis: Prompt elective or urgent repair has a good outcome, but the high emergency presentation rate and frequent need for bowel resection mean femoral hernias carry greater morbidity and mortality than inguinal hernias, especially in elderly patients.
pitfalls: Confusing a femoral hernia with an inguinal hernia and adopting a conservative approach
Missing a small femoral hernia in an obese patient presenting with unexplained bowel obstruction
Overlooking a Richter's hernia because bowel obstruction is absent despite strangulation
Delaying repair given the disproportionately high strangulation risk
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Recommend prompt surgical repair for essentially all femoral hernias given the high strangulation risk, rather than conservative management
Perform elective or urgent repair by an open or laparoscopic approach with reduction of contents and closure of the femoral canal, often with mesh
Undertake emergency surgery for incarceration or strangulation, resecting non-viable bowel where ischaemia is found
Provide preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids, analgesia and nasogastric decompression in obstruction, checking lactate where strangulation is suspected
Maintain a low threshold for exploration because a Richter's hernia can strangulate and cause ischaemia without complete bowel obstruction
Refer urgently to general surgery and expedite treatment in elderly or comorbid patients who carry greater morbidity and mortality
